HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bedroom Routines — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bedroom’s day: five routines that happen in one room from morning to night, each one owned by the child who does it.

What is this?

The bedroom routines run twice daily: make the bed and open the curtains in the morning; get dressed, read the book and turn off the light at night.

What does it mean?

A made bed is the day’s first finished task and the room’s nightly welcome. Children who close their own day — book, light — sleep on a story that ended well.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, the bed and the curtains. The morning half takes three minutes; the night half is bedtime anyway — this lesson borrows it and names it.

Why this matters

Morning jobs done in the bedroom mean the room is already won before breakfast. And the night job is the lesson’s secret: turning off the light is the child saying the day is complete.

What it teaches

Task completion (pillows first, blanket up, done), daily responsibility, and the closing ritual that tells the body the day is over.

Words to learn

make the bedcurtainsget dressedreadturn off the light

Say this to your child

“"Bedroom routines! Morning: bed made, curtains open — the room is ready. Night: book read, light off — the room is sleeping. You ran the whole day in one room."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card in the morning: "the bedroom has jobs — here are all five."
  2. Make the bed together: pillows first, blanket up, corners as best they land. Announce it finished.
  3. Open the curtains: hello, day — the room is awake.
  4. At night, get dressed for bed, then the book: one story on the made bed.
  5. The child turns off the light — the fifth word, the last move, the room sleeps.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Bedroom Routines" sit over a bed being made, blue curtains opening on a window, a folded shirt and trousers, an open book and a bedside lamp with a hand reaching for the switch.

Ask your child

"What do we do first in the bedroom?" (make the bed) "What opens the morning?" (the curtains) "What is the very last thing at night?" (turn off the light)

What your child can say or do

Your child might make the bed with military pride and forbid all sitting on it, read the book aloud to the blanket, or turn the light off with a ceremonial flourish.

Out in the real world

The made bed follows the child to every sleepover and hotel — the job travels. So does the closing ritual: book, light, goodnight, wherever the pillow is.

Try it together

Room Flip: time the morning half — bed and curtains, together, from lights-on to done. Beat yesterday’s time by a smile, not a stopwatch. The room flips itself eventually.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we make in the morning?" (the bed) "What do we open?" (the curtains) "What closes the day?" (the light going off)

This lesson pairs with the Bedroom Routines flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.
